content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Choose appropriate methods for making soluble salts
Describe methods using acids with metals, oxides, hydroxides, or carbonates
Describe the titration method for salts of soluble bases
Salts can be made by several different methods. The method chosen depends on whether the starting materials (metal, base, etc.) are
in water. This lesson focuses on making
Method 1: Acid + Excess Solid (Metal, Oxide, Hydroxide, or Carbonate)
Making salts when the base is
Add excess solid to acid. The solid reacts until all acid is used up. Filter off the excess.
[DIAGRAM: Steps showing: 1. Add acid to beaker, 2. Add solid gradually, 3. Unreacted solid remains, 4. Filter, 5. Evaporate filtrate, 6. Crystals form]
the acid gently in a beaker
the solid (metal/oxide/carbonate) a little at a time
gently until about half the water is gone
Excess solid easily removed by filtration
Making salts when the base is
You can't add "excess" because excess alkali would stay in solution and contaminate the salt.
Use a titration to find the exact volumes needed.
to measure a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask
Add acid slowly, swirling, until indicator changes colour
[DIAGRAM: Titration setup showing burette with acid, conical flask with alkali and indicator]
Heat solution gently to evaporate water
Test: dip glass rod in solution, crystals form on rod when ready
Leave to cool slowly (slow cooling = larger crystals)
Wash with a little cold distilled water
Dry between filter papers or in warm oven
Most salts of these are SOLUBLE:
All sodium, potassium, and ammonium salts
Describe how to prepare a pure, dry sample of copper sulfate crystals starting from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.
Pour dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker and warm gently
Add black copper oxide powder, a little at a time, stirring
Continue adding until no more dissolves (excess black powder remains)
Filter the mixture to remove excess copper oxide
Pour the blue filtrate into an evaporating basin
Heat gently to evaporate some water
Test by dipping a glass rod - crystals should form on it
Filter to collect the blue crystals
Explain why the titration method is used to make sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution.
Sodium hydroxide is soluble in water (it's an alkali)
If we added excess NaOH, it would remain dissolved in the solution
The salt would be contaminated with unreacted alkali
Titration allows us to find the exact volumes for complete neutralisation
We can then mix these exact volumes without indicator
This produces pure sodium chloride solution for crystallisation
A student wants to make zinc chloride. Suggest two different methods and starting materials.
Add excess zinc to dilute hydrochloric acid
Add excess zinc oxide to dilute hydrochloric acid
Using excess alkali and trying to filter it off
Alkalis dissolve - you can't filter them. Use titration instead.
Forgetting to repeat titration without indicator
Indicator would colour the salt crystals.
Gentle heating prevents spitting and decomposition.

a) What acid would they use? (1 mark)

Describe the steps in a titration to find the volume of acid needed to neutralise 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide. (5 marks)
Why are crystals washed with cold water after filtering? (2 marks)
